abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) are increasingly used to represent adaptive immune receptors, yet their advantage over classical sequence comparison remains unclear. We benchmarked general and receptor-specific PLMs against classical sequence-comparison methods for antigen-specific nearest-neighbor retrieval across four B- and T-cell receptor databases. Using CDR3 sequences alone, classical methods consistently outperformed general PLMs: BLOSUM62 and Levenshtein exceeded ESM2 variants by 7-12 percentage points in retrieval accuracy. Among receptor-specific models, only SCEPTR and, on one database, TCR2vec matched these baselines, although both additionally encoded V-gene information. AntiBERTa2 and IgBert did not close the performance gap. Using full variable-domain sequences, alignment and PLM performance converged. Germline-reversion, region-masking, and V-gene control analyses indicated that this convergence largely reflected conserved germline-derived context, particularly V-gene identity, with limited evidence for improved extraction of antigen-specific information from the CDRs. Germline dependence also extended to SCEPTR and TCR2vec. Heavily mutated HIV-1 antibodies provided a setting-specific exception to this pattern. Random train-test splits yielded retrieval accuracy 15-28 percentage points higher than clone-aware splits, consistent with optimistic performance estimates due to clonal leakage. These findings emphasize the need for strong sequence-comparison baselines and explicit germline controls when evaluating immune-receptor representations and support clone-aware splitting as a minimum benchmark standard.
